title: an argument for the sake of heaven
hookLine: a holy book that writes down its arguments, and keeps the losing side
carry: argue to learn, not to win
tomorrow: the man who argued with God about Sodom
last: MEZUZAH · CANDLES · MENSCH · SEDER · THE GLASS · MITZVAH

lines: ONE SAYS THIS, ONE SAYS THAT.
cards: Open a page of the Talmud, the great library of the rabbis' discussions, and you'll find something you might not expect in a holy book: arguments. One rabbi says this. Another says no, that.
Then a third weighs in. And very often the side that lost is written down too, and kept, for centuries. A holy book that saves its disagreements.

teach.b: And there's a well-known pair at the center of it: Hillel and Shammai, two great teachers about two thousand years ago, and the schools of students who followed them. You met Hillel on day three.
The two schools argued for years, about prayer, about Shabbat, about how to live.

teach.h: BOTH ARE THE WORDS OF THE LIVING GOD.
teach.b: Finally, the story goes, a voice from heaven settled it: both of these are the words of the living God. And the law follows Hillel. Wait.
Both are right, but one wins? Why Hillel? Because, the story says, his students were kind and humble.
They taught Shammai's view along with their own, and even taught Shammai's first. An old teaching names the difference between a good argument and a bad one.

An argument for the sake of heaven will last, and its example is Hillel and Shammai. An argument to win, to beat someone, won't. Remember the slanted mezuzah from day one: an argument where nobody had to lose.
So when Jews argue over a text, often out loud, in pairs, across a table, it isn't a lack of faith. It's how people learn.

how: Jews study the Talmud and other texts in pairs (chavruta) or in groups, arguing out loud over the meaning; the Talmud records majority and minority opinions side by side, and its discussions are studied in yeshivas, synagogues and daily study programs.

games.q: what's inside the argument — tap the pairs.

s: the Talmud records only the winning side
the losing views are written down and kept too.
a voice from heaven said both schools spoke the words of the living God
and still, the law followed Hillel.
the law followed Hillel because his side was louder
the story says because his students were kind and humble, and taught the other side first.

games.q: two schools have argued for years. a voice from heaven says both are the words of the living God. whose view becomes the law?
o: neither; the argument goes on forever.
games.why: Hillel's, the story says, because his students were kind and humble, and taught Shammai's view, even before their own.

games.q: put the voice from heaven back together.
p: are the words of the living God

practice: Three breaths with the bell. First breath: someone you disagree with. Second breath: the best version of their side, put as fairly as you can.
Third breath: notice that you can hold it without letting go of your own.

wordCard.voice: Machloket. A disagreement, and in this tradition a way of learning: argued for the sake of heaven, with both sides kept. Seventh word: a week's worth.

orig.note: Hebrew: a disagreement, from a root meaning to divide, or share out.

carryVoice: Your line: argue to learn, not to win. That's week one: seven words, and what's inside each. Tomorrow, a man who argued with God himself.
